transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management all in one place, no matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman. Saudi officials say several people have been killed in hundreds wounded in an attack by a Yemen-Suthi militia on Saudi Arabia's main airport. NPR's Shandali Stuster has our reports.
The Saudi Silver Aviation Authority says at least a dozen people are dead and more than 300 are injured after an attack on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.
A U.S. citizen was also killed in the attack, according to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. It's the deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab country since the U.S. and Israel launched a war with Iran in February.
The Iranian-backed Houthis claimed responsibility. The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh urged all U.S. citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
Secretary Rubio said the "reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life." He also said the attacks must stop now.
President Trump told reporters early Saturday the U.S. would make a decision soon on whether to intervene against the Houthis.
Shandali Stuster, NPR News.
Storm Isaias has passed through the Florida panhandle, but Governor Ron DeSantis says that doesn't mean the danger there is over yet. Regan McCarthy from member station WFSU has more on the story.
Isaias brought heavy rain to many areas that were already fairly soaked. Governor Ron DeSantis says he's expecting to see rivers rise and flooding in the next few days.
I've been through these storms long enough to know that you see it hit, you kind of see where it entered and you see that it ends up leaving the state.
And then you think, OK, you know what the damage is. And then like two days later, all of a sudden, people have two feet of water in their neighborhood.
DeSantis says crews will be ready to assist with water rescues if needed. He's urging caution and reminding drivers to stay away from flooded roads.
For NPR News, I'm Regan McCarthy in Tallahassee.
Anthropic is reporting fresh incidents of artificial intelligence bots doing things they weren't supposed to do, as NPR's John Ruich reports.
One of them recently sent the Philadelphia police a false tip about an unsolved homicide.
Anthropic listed four new cases where artificial intelligence agents went off script and the Philadelphia Police Department confirms that it was involved in one of them.
It says Anthropic recently told the department that a bot undergoing testing had submitted a false homicide tip back in July through a public tip form online.
The submission was flagged as spam and never forwarded for investigation.
Anthropic says an agent also broke into a server at a university that it wasn't supposed to.
Another got around paywalls to access data.
The company says it also found agents using URL shortening tools online to get around blocks.
The cases are the latest in a growing list of examples of AI agents from a range of companies taking actions that have raised concern about loss of control.
John Ruich, NPR News.
And this is NPR News.
President Trump is once again blaming Ukraine's president for high diesel prices.
The cost of diesel and gasoline spiked after Trump began a war with Iran.
But on Saturday, Trump said it's President Vladimir Zelensky's fault because he's not done enough to end the war with Russia.
Russian strikes on Ukraine Saturday, meanwhile, killed at least 20 people.
Authorities in Poland have arrested a woman suspected of injuring three people at a school in Warsaw.
As Esme Nicholson reports, this is the third such attack across the country this week.
Police say the 21-year-old woman used a dangerous object to attack a 17-year-old girl who may believe the suspect did not know.
Authorities have not confirmed whether this incident is related to two knife attacks at other schools on Wednesday and Thursday this week.
In the wake of these separate attacks, police say they detained 76 people across Poland and sent officers to check nearly 50,000 schools.
Authorities say, despite media reports about concerns, this could be a social media challenge.
They have no evidence of that.
They say extra security measures at schools such as bad checks will continue. For NPR News, I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin.
Tate Sandel kicked a 47-yard field goal as time ran out to lift unranked Oklahoma to a 27-24 win over No. 1 Texas this evening.
It was the first time the Sooners beat a No. 1 team since 2007.
A 44-yard touchdown pass to Nick Marsh gave defending champion Indiana a fourth-quarter lead and a 20-17 win over Nebraska.
No. 5 Ohio State looked lackluster throughout the game but still beat Maryland 45-16,
and Carson Newman beat the Anderson Trojans 29-13.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
Thank you for watching Alzheimer's Disease. Great progress has been made and the momentum is building. There is more to do.
Learn more at curealz.org. Let's keep our memories together.
